extracted.intended_audience: AISTATS 2021 paper reviewers / program committee members
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for reviewing submissions to the AISTATS 2021 conference: what reviewers should report (summary, strengths, weaknesses, correctness, clarity, relation to prior work, reproducibility, scores, ethics) and how to write constructive reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent of the review process
rubrics_metrics.description: The intent of the review process is twofold. First, to identify papers which offer significant contributions to the fields of artificial intelligence and statistics, for attendees and readers. Second, to provide constructive feedback to authors that they can use to improve their work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reviewing a paper, always think about the impact the work may have on the community in the long run—out-of-the-box ideas, novel problems and “bridging fields' contributions are crucial for the successful development of the field so do not neglect high-level picture in favor of technical correctness, which is also important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of bias against novel/interdisciplinary work
rubrics_metrics.description: Novel and/or interdisciplinary works ... are often very easy to criticize ... However, such work may be of high importance for the progress of the field in the long run, so please try to be aware of this bias, and avoid dismissive criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful not to dismiss work simply because assumptions or models are not yet widely accepted. Give fair consideration to high-level impact and new problem formulations as well as technical correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary and contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Briefly summarize the paper and its contributions. Summarize the paper motivation, key contributions and achievements in a paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although this part of the review may not provide much new information to authors, it is invaluable to ACs, and program chairs, and it can help the authors determine whether there are misunderstandings that need to be addressed in their author response. Examples of contributions that warrant publication include theoretical, methodological, algorithmic, empirical, bridge papers, or critical analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengths
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the strengths of the work. Typical criteria include: soundness of the claims (theoretical grounding, empirical evaluation), significance and novelty of the contribution, and relevance to the AISTATS community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List the strengths of the submission; e.g., soundness of theoretical claims, sound empirical methodology, significance/novelty relative to literature (cite relevant prior works). One measure of significance is how much researchers or practitioners will use or be influenced by the ideas. Solid technical papers that explore new territory or point out new directions are preferable to small incremental advances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain the limitations of this work along the same axes as above.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is like strengths but focusing on limitations. Comments should be detailed, specific, and polite. Avoid vague, subjective complaints and dismissive or inappropriate language. Remember you are reviewing scientific contribution, not your personal interest in the submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctness (technical and empirical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the claims and method correct? Is the empirical methodology correct?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain if there is anything incorrect with the paper. Incorrect claims or methodology are the primary reason for rejection. Be detailed, specific and polite. Thoroughly motivate criticisms so authors can understand and respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the paper well written?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rate clarity of exposition and give examples of what parts of the paper need revision to improve clarity. A superbly written paper provides enough information for an expert reader to reproduce results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation to prior work
rubrics_metrics.description: Is it clearly discussed how this work differs from previous contributions?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain whether the submission adequately relates to prior literature. The related work section should not just list prior work but explain differences. Authors are excused for not knowing all non-refereed work (e.g., ArXiv). Papers appearing less than two months before the submission deadline are considered contemporaneous and authors are not obligated to make detailed comparisons to such papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Are there enough details to reproduce the major results of this work?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark whether the work is not reproducible, some aspects are reproducible, or most aspects are reproducible. Lack of reproducibility should be listed among the weaknesses of the submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional feedback, suggestions and questions (optional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Add here any additional comment you might have about the submission, including questions and suggestions for improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this field to provide constructive comments, suggestions for experiments or analyses, and questions for the authors that can help improve the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall score
rubrics_metrics.description: Overall Score should reflect your assessment of the submission's contributions. Do not assume your assigned sample is representative nor adjust to match conference acceptance rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numeric scale and guidance: 10 = Top 5% of accepted AISTATS papers (truly groundbreaking); 9 = Top 15% (excellent); 8 = Top 50% (very good); 7 = Good (accept; wouldn't be upset if rejected); 6 = Marginally above acceptance threshold (tend to accept); 5 = Marginally below threshold (tend to reject); 4 = Okay but not good enough (reject); 3 = Clear reject; 2 = Strong reject (surprised it was submitted); 1 = Trivial, wrong, or already known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidence score
rubrics_metrics.description: How certain you are about your assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 5 = absolutely certain; very familiar with related work. 4 = confident but not absolute. 3 = fairly confident; possible unfamiliarity or un-checked math. 2 = willing to defend but likely unfamiliar with central parts. 1 = educated guess; not in your area or hard to understand; math not carefully checked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical concerns flag
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the submission raise potential ethical concerns? This includes methods, applications, or data that create or reinforce unfair bias or that have a primary purpose of harm or injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Yes or No. Your rating should be independent of this. If Yes, briefly explain the potential ethical concerns. Flagging may indicate need for additional review from the ethics perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation of ethical concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: If the submission raises potential ethical concerns, briefly explain the potential concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concise explanation of methods, applications, or data issues that create/reinforce bias or harm and why they are concerning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement to abide by AISTATS code of conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Agree to abide by the AISTATS code of conduct
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers must agree to the code of conduct. The AISTATS Code of Conduct is linked from the guideline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidential comments to Area Chair (optional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Confidential comments for the Area Chair (optional).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use for comments you wish to keep confidential from the authors (explicit comparisons to other submissions, blunt criticisms). If you accidentally learn author identities, do not divulge them here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive feedback principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide constructive feedback that accounts for both strengths and weaknesses and helps ACs and authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a list of arguments for and against acceptance, justify scope/out-of-scope judgements, be precise when citing prior work, and suggest concrete improvements. Avoid only listing weaknesses; recognize strengths as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality (support for claims / completeness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the submission technically sound? Are claims well supported by theoretical analysis or experimental results? Is this a complete piece of work or work in progress?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether claims are supported, whether authors are careful and honest in evaluating strengths and weaknesses. Cite specific technical issues or missing validations where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the tasks or methods new? Is the work a novel combination of well-known techniques? Is it clear how this work differs from previous contributions?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate novelty relative to prior work and whether related work is adequately cited. Note when related or contemporaneous work is missing in citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the results important? Are others likely to use the ideas or build on them? Does the submission address a difficult task better than previous work?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the paper advances the state of the art, provides unique data or approaches, or yields unique conclusions. Judge the practical or theoretical impact on the community.
